title: Armalyte
build: Thalamus disk release, two G64 side images (a verified dump, marked (!)) from the C64 Preservation Project's 10th Anniversary Collection on the Internet Archive; sha256 of each side in orientation.md

The ending, run from $0801 when the eighth level is finished ($B3CC with $B002 = 8): a program of its own that shows five pictures in a frame, each with a message typed out under it, then waits for RUN/STOP and goes back to the front end for the next round. It takes over the machine: interrupts off, stack at $0112, I/O in and both ROMs out ($01 = $35), screen and sprites off, a black border and background, zero page $02-$FF cleared. Then it copies the frame's colours ($4D08-$4FFF) to colour RAM rows 0-18 and blanks the six text rows below ($7EF8-$7FE7, colour 8).
In a level file, the unpacker's entry, where the fast loader jumps once the file is in ($0812); here the high byte of the STA $D011 above.

Moves the frame picture up by $1000, from $5000-$6EF8 to $6000-$7EF8, a byte at a time from the top down through the patched LDA/STA below, so the bitmap lands at $6000, the text font at $7800 and the frame's screen colours at $7C00. The check on the destination's high byte ($0865, which ends at $5F) makes a second run skip the move.
Low byte of the byte being moved, the operand of LDA $6EF8 at $0860, counted down by frame_move_up.
High byte of the byte being moved, from $6E down to $4F.
Low byte of where it goes, the operand of STA $7EF8 at $0863.
High byte of where it goes, from $7E down to $5F; the loop stops below $60, and a second run of the ending finds it there and skips the move.

Sets the ending's display: IRQ vector $0998 and NMI vector $09AE (an RTI, so RESTORE does nothing), video bank 1 ($DD00 = 2, $4000-$7FFF), multicolour ($D016 = $D8), screen at $7C00 and bitmap at $6000 (or characters at $7800 in text mode) through $D018 = $FE; the interrupt's first stage ($09AF), the raster interrupt on, colours held for the first fade ($0F = 1) and tune 2 of the music driver. Then it shows picture 0 ($08FA).

Waits for the picture's short pause ($07/$08) to run out, then gives it about fifteen seconds ($08 = 3: three times 256 frames) while watching the joystick in port 2 and the keyboard: fire, or the time running out, moves to the next picture; RUN/STOP (row 7, column 7 of the keyboard) skips to the last.
Holds the colours for the fade ($0F = 1) and moves on a picture ($06); after the fifth it goes to the last wait ($0923).
Shows picture $06 while it is below 5 ($097D), otherwise goes to the last wait.
RUN/STOP: goes straight to the fifth picture (number 4), shown in full here, unless it is already up.

After the last picture: waits 16 frames, then keeps the music going (tune 0 again whenever the driver has stopped, $C057 = 0) until RUN/STOP is pressed. Then it fades the music out ($C058 = 0: one volume step a frame) and waits for it to stop, gives the machine back to the front end's settings (processor port $2F/$36, CIA 2 port A, keyboard ports, CIA interrupts off) and enters the front end ($B030) with level 1 next ($B002 = 0) and $B004 = 0, so the load ends at "PRESS FIRE TO START" and the game goes on, score and lives kept, one round faster ($B02D).
An STA $06 that nothing reaches: the code before it ends with JMP $B030 and the branch at $08FE goes past it to $097D.

Shows picture $06: fades the window from bright to black ($0BE8), copies the picture's bitmap in while it is black ($0AC1), clears the text rows ($0C37), types the message ($0C42), fades the window from black up to white ($0B97), lets the interrupt take the picture's own text colours ($0F = 0) and puts in the picture's colours, which reveals it ($0B01). A five-frame pause, then the wait for input.
The ending's raster interrupt: keeps A, X and Y in $03-$05, acknowledges the video chip, and jumps through the address at $09A4, which ending_screen_on points at the stage switch ($09AF).
Low byte of where ending_irq goes on, the operand of JMP at $09A3: $AF, for $09AF.
High byte of where ending_irq goes on: $09.
Gets A, X and Y back from $03-$05 and returns from the interrupt; the LDA #$00 before them is overwritten at once. The RTI at $09AE is also the NMI handler.

Alternates the interrupt's two stages ($02 = 0, 1): sets the raster line for the next one from $09CB ($CA, then $20) and jumps to this one's handler through the patched JMP at $09C8 (addresses from $09CF/$09D1): $09D3 at line $20, $0A06 at line $CA.
Low byte of the stage handler, the operand of JMP at $09C8, patched from $09CF.
High byte of the stage handler, patched from $09D1.

The interrupt's stages: the raster line to ask for next ($CA, $20) at $09CB, then the handlers' low bytes ($D3, $06) at $09CF and high bytes ($09, $0A) at $09D1, so the handler at $09D3 runs at line $20 and the one at $0A06 at line $CA.
The stage handlers' low bytes, $D3 and $06, read by ending_irq_stage.
The stage handlers' high bytes, $09 and $0A.

At line $20, above the picture: bitmap mode ($D011 = $3B) on a black background. Unless a fade holds them ($0F), takes picture $06's three text colours from $0E7B/$0E80/$0E85 into $10-$12. Counts the typing delay $0B down and plays the music ($C059).

At line $CA, just above character row 19: text mode ($D011 = $1B) for the six text rows, with the text colours $10, $11 and $12 into $D023, $D021 and $D022; counts the picture timer $07/$08 down, $07 every frame and $08 each time $07 runs out.

Where each of the 20 character rows of the bitmap starts, from $6000, 320 bytes apart and 80 bytes in (column 10, where the picture window begins): low bytes here, high bytes at $0A41. Rows 3-14 are the window's.
High bytes of the 20 bitmap rows' window addresses.
Where each of the 25 screen rows starts at column 10 of the screen at $7C00: low bytes here, high bytes at $0A6E. The same low byte with $D8 in place of $7C gives the colour-RAM address.
High bytes of the 25 screen rows' column-10 addresses ($7C-$7F).
Low bytes of the five pictures' bitmaps, by picture number; high bytes at $0A8C: $0F00, $17E8, $20D0, $29B8, $32A0, 2,280 bytes apart.
High bytes of the five pictures' bitmaps.
Low bytes of the five pictures' screen colours (each 1,920 bytes after its bitmap); high bytes at $0A96.
High bytes of the five pictures' screen colours.
Low bytes of the five pictures' packed colour-RAM colours (240 bytes after the screen colours); high bytes at $0AA0.
High bytes of the five pictures' colour-RAM colours.
The window's fade, six steps from black (0) to bright (5): what each step writes into all of the window's screen colours (00 00 00 0B 0C BC), and the text's $D021 colour ($11).
What each fade step writes into the window's colour RAM (00 0B 0C 01 01 01), and the text's $D023 colour ($10).
Each fade step's third text colour, for $D022 ($12): black, then dark grey at the last step.
Low bytes of the five messages' addresses, by picture; high bytes at $0ABC: $0C8C, $0CDF, $0D22, $0D7C, $0E04.
High bytes of the five messages' addresses.

Copies picture $06's bitmap into the window: twelve rows (3-14) of 160 bytes, from the picture's address ($0A87/$0A8C) to each row's place ($0A2D/$0A41), through the patched LDA/STA at $0ADF and $0AE2, the source moving on 160 bytes a row.
LDA from the picture's bitmap: its operand ($0AE0/$0AE1) is patched with the source, and moves on 160 bytes a row; the $0ADF it holds before that is never used.
Low byte of the bitmap source, set from $0A87 and moved on by 160 each row.
High byte of the bitmap source, from $0A8C.
STA into the window's row: its operand ($0AE3/$0AE4) is patched from the bitmap row tables.
Low byte of the window row being written, from $0A2D.
High byte of the window row being written, from $0A41.

Puts picture $06's colours in, which makes it appear: 20 screen colours for each window row (3-14) from $0A91/$0A96 to the screen at $7C00, then the colour-RAM colours from $0A9B/$0AA0, packed two to a byte (low nibble first), 10 bytes unpacked to 20 cells of each row.
LDA from the picture's screen colours, patched through $0B2C/$0B2D.
Low byte of the screen-colour source, from $0A91, moved on 20 a row.
High byte of the screen-colour source, from $0A96.
STA to the screen row, patched through $0B2F/$0B30 from $0A55/$0A6E.
Low byte of the screen row being written.
High byte of the screen row being written.

The colour-RAM half of picture_reveal: for each window row, 10 packed bytes from $0A9B/$0AA0, each written to two cells, the byte itself and then, rotated four places, its high nibble; the row's colour-RAM address is its screen address with $D8 in place of $7C.
LDA from the packed colours, patched through $0B6B/$0B6C.
Low byte of the packed-colour source, from $0A9B, moved on 10 a row.
High byte of the packed-colour source, from $0AA0.
STA of the low nibble into colour RAM, patched through $0B6E/$0B6F.
Low byte of the colour-RAM row, from $0A55.
High byte of the colour-RAM row: the screen row's high byte's low two bits with $D8.
STA of the high nibble into the next cell, patched through $0B76/$0B77 with the same row.
Low byte of the colour-RAM row for the high nibbles.
High byte of the colour-RAM row for the high nibbles.

Fades the window from black up to bright: six steps (0-5) three frames apart, each filling the window's twelve rows (20 cells each) with that step's screen colour ($0AA5) and colour-RAM colour ($0AAB), and setting the text colours $10-$12 to match.
STA of the fade's screen colour, patched through $0BC1/$0BC2 with the row.
Low byte of the screen row fade_up fills.
High byte of the screen row fade_up fills.
STA of the fade's colour-RAM colour, patched through $0BC7/$0BC8.
Low byte of the colour-RAM row fade_up fills.
High byte of the colour-RAM row fade_up fills.
The same as fade_up the other way, steps 5 down to 0: the old picture turns bright and fades to black.
STA of fade_down's screen colour, patched through $0C12/$0C13.
Low byte of the screen row fade_down fills.
High byte of the screen row fade_down fills.
STA of fade_down's colour-RAM colour, patched through $0C18/$0C19.
Low byte of the colour-RAM row fade_down fills.
High byte of the colour-RAM row fade_down fills.
Clears the five message rows, 20-24 ($7F20-$7FE7), to character 0, which is solid black: all its bit pairs take the colour-RAM colour, black in these rows.

Types picture $06's message (address from $0AB7/$0ABC) into the text rows, one character a frame ($0B). Its first byte is where the text starts, less one ($FF: row 20, column 0); then each byte is a character of the ending's font, $11 moves to the start of the next row, and $10 ends it. A message stops at 200 characters.
$11: moves X to the last column of the row it is in (39, 79, ... through the CPX # at $0C7D, whose operand is patched), so the next character starts the next row.
The operand of CPX # at $0C7D, set to $27 and moved on 40 at a time by message_newline until it passes the cursor.

Picture 0's message: the start less one ($FF), then the text in the font's codes (the letters' ASCII values), with $11 for each new row and $10 at the end: "DELTA PROBE TO WOODWARD, / OUTER DEFENCES NEUTRALIZED, / RESISTANCE IS LIGHT ..."

Picture 1's message: the start less one ($FF), then the text in the font's codes (the letters' ASCII values), with $11 for each new row and $10 at the end: "APPROACHING DOCKING BAY 12, / H'SIFFAN RESISTANCE ANTICIPATED ..."

Picture 2's message: the start less one ($FF), then the text in the font's codes (the letters' ASCII values), with $11 for each new row and $10 at the end: "DOCKING SUCCESSFUL, / NO H'SIFFAN RESISTANCE ENCOUNTERED, / THE COMPLEX IS DESERTED ..."

Picture 3's message: the start less one ($FF), then the text in the font's codes (the letters' ASCII values), with $11 for each new row and $10 at the end: "CERBERUS NOW UNDER OUR CONTROL. / WOODWARD TO DELTA PROBE: / THANKYOU, TEN BILLION CYBER CREDITS / HAVE BEEN TRANSFERRED TO YOUR ACCOUNT."

Picture 4's message: the start less one ($FF), then the text in the font's codes (the letters' ASCII values), with $11 for each new row and $10 at the end: "CONGRATULATIONS, / DELTA II MISSION COMPLETE, / PREPARE FOR TEMPORAL SHIFT ! / (PRESS RUN/STOP TO CONTINUE YOUR GAME)"

Each picture's three text colours, for the message rows below it: $D023 here (white for all five), $D021 at $0E80 (light blue, light red, green, grey, orange) and $D022 at $0E85 (blue, brown, brown, dark grey, brown).
Each picture's text colour for $D021: light blue, light red, green, grey, orange.
Each picture's text colour for $D022: blue, brown, brown, dark grey, brown.

Picture 0's bitmap, two ships flying right along a corridor of machinery: rows 3-8 of the window (the top half), 160 bytes a character row, 20 cells of 8 bytes, copied into the frame by picture_copy_bitmap.
Picture 0's bitmap from the 256th byte on (at $1000), in window row 4.
Picture 0's bitmap, rows 9-14 of the window (the lower half).
In a level this address ($142C) holds the wave flags by tile column, which the engine refers to; the ending, where the engine does not run, has picture 0's bitmap here.
In a level this address ($152C) holds the wave numbers, which the engine refers to; the ending, where the engine does not run, has picture 0's bitmap here.
In a level this address ($162C) holds the wave sizes, which the engine refers to; the ending, where the engine does not run, has picture 0's bitmap here.

Picture 0's screen colours, 20 bytes for each of the window's twelve rows: each byte gives a cell's colours for the bit pairs 01 (high nibble) and 10 (low nibble), copied to $7C0A on by picture_reveal.
In a level this address ($172C) holds the wave lists' high bytes, which the engine refers to; the ending, where the engine does not run, has picture 0's screen colours here.
Picture 0's colour-RAM colours, the colour of each cell's bit pair 11, packed two cells to a byte (low nibble first), 10 bytes a row, unpacked to $D80A on by picture_reveal.

Picture 1's bitmap, a space station with a ship in its window and an explosion at its lower right: rows 3-8 of the window (the top half), 160 bytes a character row, 20 cells of 8 bytes, copied into the frame by picture_copy_bitmap.

Picture 1's bitmap, rows 9-14 of the window (the lower half).

In a level this address ($45D3) holds the scoreboard sprite where player 1's generator count is drawn, which the engine refers to; the ending, where the engine does not run, has zeros the ending never reads here.
The byte before the frame's colours, nothing of its own: ending_start reads $4D07 + X with X from $BE down to 1, so its first quarter starts at $4D08.
The frame's colour-RAM colours, 19 rows of 40 (only the low nibble counts), copied to $D800-$DAF7 by ending_start before anything is shown.
The last byte of the frame colours' first quarter ($4D08-$4DC5, to $D800-$D8BD); ending_start reads $4DC5 + X for the second, $4DC6-$4E83 to $D8BE-$D97B.
The last byte of the second quarter; ending_start reads $4E83 + X for the third, $4E84-$4F41 to $D97C-$DA39.
The last byte of the third quarter; ending_start reads $4F41 + X for the fourth, $4F42-$4FFF to $DA3A-$DAF7.
The frame picture's bitmap, character rows 0-2 (320 bytes a row), moved to $6000 on by frame_move_up: the yellow pipes, panels and grilles around the window.

The frame picture's bitmap, character rows 3-5 (320 bytes a row), moved to $63C0 on by frame_move_up: the yellow pipes, panels and grilles around the window (rows 3-14 of columns 10-29, the window, are overwritten by each picture).

The messages' font, characters $00-$5A in multicolour, moved to $7800 by frame_move_up: character 0 and the space are solid in the colour-RAM colour (black), and the letters and signs are drawn in the three text colours, at their ASCII codes.

Zeros in the load, after the font. Once frame_move_up has run, $6000-$77BF is the frame's bitmap, so these addresses hold its rows 8-9 (moved up from $5AD8-$5BFF), and picture_copy_bitmap writes window rows 8 and 9 into them.

Zeros in the load, after the frame's screen colours; frame_move_up starts at $6EF8. After the move these addresses hold the frame bitmap's rows 11-12 (from $5EF8-$5FFF), where picture_copy_bitmap writes window rows 11 and 12.
